d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
Benefits are unknown but the hope is for improved neurological symptoms, tumor shrinkage and improved quality of life.


Your pet may not get any benefit from being in this research study. This treatment has a sound medical basis but is the subject of this clinical trial because it has not been used in animals in the same way as it is being tested in this study. Your pet’s disease may get better, stay the same, or get worse while participating in this study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks:
Risks associated with blood draws

The risk of blood draws and catheter placement include discomfort, mild redness, bruising, and very rarely infection at the site of blood sampling. In some cases, it is necessary to clip the hair over the vein in order to facilitate collection of a blood sample.


Risks of general anesthesia

Anesthetic drugs often affect blood pressure, heart rate, breathing, and body temperature; we monitor vital signs continuously during and after anesthesia. Complications can happen, but life-threatening ones are uncommon. The complications include decreased heart rate and blood pressure, poor oxygenation and tissue perfusion (cyanosis), trauma to the respiratory tract due to intubation, aspiration pneumonia, gastrointestinal upset (such as vomiting and diarrhea), catheter site inflammation and infection, acute kidney injury, allergy to anesthetic drugs, cardiopulmonary arrest, and death. You can ask to discuss the risks with your care provider team prior to the anesthetic event, and you will be asked to sign the hospital’s standard consent form for general anesthesia during the visit.


Risks of radiation therapy for brain tumors

Radiation therapy is commonly used to treat brain tumors in dogs and is generally well tolerated. However, side effects can occur. Some side effects happen during or shortly after treatment, while others may develop weeks to months later. Because FLASH proton radiation therapy is still being studied, there may also be risks or side effects that are not yet known.


Acute Side Effects (during treatment to approximately 3 months after treatment): These side effects are usually temporary and can often be managed with medications. Rarely, they can be unresponsive to medical management and life-threatening.

Signs may include:

  1. Tiredness or decreased activity
  2. Reduced appetite or nausea
  3. Temporary swelling of the brain because of inflammation and edema, which may cause worsening of neurologic signs such as seizures, weakness, imbalance, behavior changes, or decreased alertness.
  4. In rare cases, severe brain swelling requires hospitalization or intensive care.


Delayed Acute Side Effects (weeks to a few months after treatment): Some dogs experience temporary worsening of neurologic signs after an initial period of improvement.

Signs may include:

  1. New or worsening seizures
  2. Weakness or difficulty walking
  3. Changes in behavior
  4. Reduced alertness or confusion


These changes are often treated with medications such as corticosteroids and may improve over time.


Late Side Effects (more than 3 months after treatment, usually months to years after): Late side effects are less common but may be permanent.

Signs may include:

  1. Persistent or new neurologic problems, including seizures, weakness, balance problems, vision changes, or behavior changes.
  2. Damage to normal brain tissue (radiation necrosis) or stroke-like injury, which may cause symptoms similar to those caused by the tumor.
  3. Although uncommon, severe radiation-related complications can significantly affect quality of life and, in rare cases, may be life-threatening.


Your dog will be monitored closely throughout the study with physical examinations, neurologic evaluations, and MRI scans.

If significant side effects occur, appropriate treatment will be provided, and your dog may be withdrawn from the study if continued participation is no longer in their best interest.


Potential risks associated with Gilvetmab

Gilvetmab is a specific antibody, a special protein made by the immune system, to find and destroy germs like bacteria and viruses, that aims to enhance a dog’s ability for its’ own immune system to attack cancer cells.

In healthy and cancer-bearing dogs who had previously received Gilvetmab, negative side-effects were mostly mild, resolved with treatment, and occurred in less than 40% of patients.


The negative side effects include lethargy/fatigue, reduced appetite, vomiting, weight loss, increased liver enzymes (ALP, ALT, AST), anemia (low red blood cells), nausea, proteinuria (increased protein in the urine), tumor hemorrhage (bleeding) or hypotension (low blood pressure, but only in dogs with mast cell tumor), hypersensitivity/allergic reaction, anaphylaxis, muscle weakness, tremor. Based on human medicine experience, autoimmune disease can occur with ICIs; examples are listed below, but clinically, these immune-related diseases have not been reported in the previous canine clinical trial.


There is a possibility that your dog’s immune cells could not only attack your dog’s cancer cells but also other cells in your dog’s body. This condition, in which immune cells begin to attack your own tissues, is known as “autoimmune disease.” Autoimmune disease can affect many parts of the body, such as the skin, kidneys, nerves, muscles, the endocrine system (the system that directs the body’s hormones and other chemicals), and the digestive system (gut). If your dog develops an autoimmune disease, he/she will need to be treated with corticosteroids alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive drugs to try to prevent immune cells from damaging healthy tissues. If your dog were to develop an autoimmune disease, they may be removed from the study on a case-by-case basis.


Please note: There may also be unknown risks that are not yet identified. If your pet becomes ill, you should inform any veterinarian that your pet is participating in a research study.


Risks of obtaining tumor biopsies in the brain (optional)

A brain tumor biopsy involves removing a small sample of the tumor using a needle-like or surgical instrument while your dog is under general anesthesia. Although this procedure is commonly performed by experienced veterinary specialists, it carries risks because the brain is a sensitive organ.


Possible risks include:

- Bleeding within or around the brain, which may cause neurologic problems and, in rare cases, require emergency treatment.

- Swelling of the brain, which can temporarily or permanently worsen neurologic signs.

- Infection, although this is uncommon because the procedure is performed using sterile techniques.

- Temporary or permanent neurologic changes, such as weakness, difficulty walking, vision changes, changes in behavior, or seizures, depending on the location of the tumor.

- Failure to obtain a diagnostic sample, meaning the biopsy may not provide enough tissue to make a diagnosis or complete all planned research tests.

- Death, although extremely uncommon, is a potential risk of any invasive brain procedure.

Your dog's imaging studies will be carefully reviewed before the biopsy, and the procedure will only be performed by experienced veterinary neurosurgeons. If, at the time of the procedure, the biopsy is considered unsafe, it will not be performed.

Risks of collecting cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

CSF collection is a commonly performed procedure in veterinary neurology and is generally considered safe when performed by experienced clinicians. However, as with any medical procedure, there are some risks. Possible risks include:

- Mild pain or soreness at the collection site after the procedure

- Temporary worsening of neurologic signs, such as weakness, imbalance, or seizures

- Bleeding at the collection site or, rarely, around the brain or spinal cord

- Infection, although this is uncommon because sterile techniques are used

- Temporary leakage of spinal fluid, which usually resolves on its own

- In very rare cases, severe neurologic complications, including brain herniation (movement of brain tissue due to increased pressure inside the skull), paralysis, coma, or death


Before collecting CSF, your dog will undergo brain imaging (MRI) to help determine whether the procedure can be performed safely. If the procedure is considered unsafe, it will not be performed.


Risks of Urine Collection

We will collect a urine sample whenever possible using a free-catch method, which means collecting urine while your dog urinates naturally. There are no known risks associated with collecting a free-catch urine sample. If a free-catch sample cannot be obtained, or is not suitable for testing, we may recommend cystocentesis. Cystocentesis is a standard veterinary procedure involving the sterile collection of a urine sample by inserting a needle into the urinary bladder through the abdominal wall. Risks of this procedure can include: discomfort, mild redness, bruising or bleeding, leaking of urine in the abdomen, and, very rarely, infection at the site of urine collection.
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
1. Histopathologic confirmation of glioma by a board-certified veterinary pathologist or diagnostic MRI indicating a supratentorial lesion consistent with glioma.
  2. No major underlying health conditions that would make patient high risk to undergo general anesthesia.
  3. Tumor size and presentation amendable to FLASH RT equipment.
  4. Has not received systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy in the past 3 weeks.
  5. Has never received Gilvetmab before.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
1. Respiratory distress
  2. Neurological symptoms grade 3 (stupor or non-ambulatory) or grade 2 at clinician discretion
  3. High risk for anesthesia
  4. History of immune-mediated disease or significant co-morbidities
  5. Contraindicated to Gilvetmab or received Gilvetmab before
  6. Client unable to travel to Philadelphia, PA for all study visits
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name: FLASH proton radiation therapy (FLASH-RT) administered either alone or in combination with Gilvetmab
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_name: Patient survival time, change in neurological symptoms
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Neurological examinations, MRIs, Grading criteria such as iRECIST guidelines, RANO 2.0, VCOG-CTCAE v2 and VRTOG v2
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint: At any point a patient may discontinue participation in the trial. If their symptoms worsen and/or it is unsafe for them to go under general anesthesia, enrollment will stop.
